summary: This standards-track memo defines an IP option that tells routers along a packet's path to look at it more closely than usual. It is useful for protocols that need routers to process certain packets even though they are not addressed to the router.

eli5.summary: A flag on a letter saying every post office on the way should read this one carefully.

questions: how to make routers inspect a packet
what is the ip router alert option
what is router alert option number
subtitle: An IP option that tells routers to look more closely at a packet that is not addressed to them.

tldr.problem: Protocols such as RSVP need routers to intercept packets not addressed to them, but changing the main forwarding path could cost too much performance.
tldr.mechanism: The Router Alert IP option (option number 20, length 4) marks a packet so routers that recognize it examine it more closely, while ordinary forwarding is untouched.
tldr.outcome: It lets new protocols like RSVP and IGMP get router attention cheaply. It has been updated by RFC 5350 and RFC 6398.

today: RFC 2113 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 5350 and RFC 6398.

sections.title: Why Routers Need an Alert
sections.content:
New protocols often couple loosely to unicast routing, so they know only the next hop toward the destination. Phased deployment is hard, because a router cannot easily find other routers that speak the new protocol. RSVP gets around this by addressing packets to the final destination and asking routers to make a small change in their forwarding path to pull out RSVP packets.

That small change can be costly, since the mainline forwarding path is highly tuned, and a single extra instruction may cost hundreds of packets per second.
sections.eli5: Checking every package for a special sign would slow the mail down. A visible flag lets only the flagged ones get a second look.

sections.title: The Router Alert Option
sections.content:
The option has the semantic that routers should examine this packet more closely. Its type byte is 10010100: copied flag 1 (all fragments carry it), option class 0 (control) and option number 20. The length is 4, followed by a two-octet value. Value 0 means the router shall examine the packet, and values 1 to 65535 are reserved.

Routers that handle options in the fast path already branch on option type. Routers that do not will push such packets to the slow path, so regular data packets see no penalty.
sections.eli5: The flag is a few bytes in the packet header. A zero value in it says please read this one.

sections.title: Semantics and Security Notes
sections.content:
Hosts shall ignore the option. Routers that do not recognize it shall ignore it. Routers that do recognize it shall examine the packet more closely, such as checking the IP Protocol field, to decide if more processing is needed. Unrecognized values are silently ignored. Its use must be mandated in protocols that rely on it; the RFC names RSVP and IGMP.

The security considerations are about misuse: if the option is missing when needed, the protocol suffers, and if it is set when not needed, the packet is processed more slowly.
sections.eli5: Houses ignore the flag. Post offices that know it read the letter. If you flag everything, the mail gets slow.

fields.name: Value
fields.desc: 0 means router shall examine packet; 1-65535 reserved.
